claim: Loss of Foxc1 is associated with Dandy-Walker malformation.
source: Loss of Foxc1 is associated with Dandy-Walker malformation, the most common human cerebellar malformation characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa and fourth ventricle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established association.

claim: Dandy-Walker malformation is the most common human cerebellar malformation.
source: Loss of Foxc1 is associated with Dandy-Walker malformation, the most common human cerebellar malformation characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa and fourth ventricle.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: Dandy-Walker malformation is characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa and fourth ventricle.
source: Loss of Foxc1 is associated with Dandy-Walker malformation, the most common human cerebellar malformation characterized by cerebellar hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa and fourth ventricle.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic in the abstract.

claim: Foxc1 is expressed in the mouse posterior fossa mesenchyme.
source: Although expressed in the mouse posterior fossa mesenchyme, loss of Foxc1 non-autonomously induces a rapid and devastating decrease in embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone radial glial proliferation and concurrent increase in cerebellar neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observed expression pattern.

claim: Loss of Foxc1 non-autonomously induces a rapid and devastating decrease in embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone radial glial proliferation.
source: Although expressed in the mouse posterior fossa mesenchyme, loss of Foxc1 non-autonomously induces a rapid and devastating decrease in embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone radial glial proliferation and concurrent increase in cerebellar neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of Foxc1 induces a concurrent increase in cerebellar neuronal differentiation.
source: Although expressed in the mouse posterior fossa mesenchyme, loss of Foxc1 non-autonomously induces a rapid and devastating decrease in embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone radial glial proliferation and concurrent increase in cerebellar neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Migration of cerebellar neurons is disrupted in Foxc1 mutants.
source: Subsequent migration of cerebellar neurons is disrupted, associated with disordered radial glial morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observed phenotype.

claim: Disrupted cerebellar neuronal migration is associated with disordered radial glial morphology.
source: Subsequent migration of cerebellar neurons is disrupted, associated with disordered radial glial morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an observed correlation.

claim: SDF1α is a direct Foxc1 target.
source: In vitro, SDF1α, a direct Foxc1 target also expressed in the head mesenchyme, acts as a cerebellar radial glial mitogen and a chemoattractant for nascent Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Zarbalis et al., 2012 in the main text.

claim: SDF1α is expressed in the head mesenchyme.
source: In vitro, SDF1α, a direct Foxc1 target also expressed in the head mesenchyme, acts as a cerebellar radial glial mitogen and a chemoattractant for nascent Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: SDF1α acts as a cerebellar radial glial mitogen in vitro.
source: In vitro, SDF1α, a direct Foxc1 target also expressed in the head mesenchyme, acts as a cerebellar radial glial mitogen and a chemoattractant for nascent Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: SDF1α acts as a chemoattractant for nascent Purkinje cells in vitro.
source: In vitro, SDF1α, a direct Foxc1 target also expressed in the head mesenchyme, acts as a cerebellar radial glial mitogen and a chemoattractant for nascent Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro experimental data.

claim: Cxcr4 is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells.
source: Its receptor, Cxcr4, is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells and conditional Cxcr4 ablation with Nes-Cre mimics the Foxc1−/− cerebellar phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including immunohistochemistry and transgenic reporter mice.

claim: Conditional Cxcr4 ablation with Nes-Cre mimics the Foxc1−/− cerebellar phenotype.
source: Its receptor, Cxcr4, is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells and conditional Cxcr4 ablation with Nes-Cre mimics the Foxc1−/− cerebellar phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing the two mutant phenotypes.

claim: SDF1α rescues the Foxc1−/− phenotype.
source: SDF1α also rescues the Foxc1−/− phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro rescue experiments.

claim: The head mesenchyme exerts a considerable influence on early embryonic brain development.
source: Our data emphasizes that the head mesenchyme exerts a considerable influence on early embryonic brain development and its disruption contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Disruption of head mesenchyme contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders in humans.
source: Our data emphasizes that the head mesenchyme exerts a considerable influence on early embryonic brain development and its disruption contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their relevance to human disease.

claim: Heterozygous loss of the Foxc1 gene contributes to DWM.
source: Heterozygous loss of the Foxc1 gene contributes to DWM.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the introduction.

claim: In mice, Foxc1 expression is limited to vascular pericytes within the developing cerebellum.
source: Although loss of this transcription factor causes significant developmental cerebellar pathology in humans and mice, in mice, its expression is limited to vascular pericytes within the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as an observed expression pattern in the introduction.

claim: Foxc1 is widely expressed in the posterior fossa mesenchyme surrounding the cerebellar anlage beginning after e12.5 in mice.
source: In contrast, Foxc1 is widely expressed in the posterior fossa mesenchyme surrounding the cerebellar anlage beginning after e12.5 in mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observed expression pattern in the introduction.

claim: Reduced mesenchymal expression of several secreted factors including Bmp 2, 4 and SDF1α occurs in the mouse Foxc1 e12.5 mutant posterior fossa.
source: We previously reported reduced mesenchymal expression of several secreted factors in the mouse Foxc1 e12.5 mutant posterior fossa including Bmp 2, 4 and SDF1α (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a previously reported finding with citation.

claim: The cerebellar anlage is derived from dorsal rhombomere 1.
source: The cerebellar anlage derived from dorsal rhombomere 1 is initially established by Fgf8 and other signalling molecules originating from the isthmic organizer, a transient embryonic mid/hindbrain junction at neural tube closure (Nakamura et al., 2005; Basson and Wingate, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The cerebellar anlage is initially established by Fgf8 and other signalling molecules originating from the isthmic organizer.
source: The cerebellar anlage derived from dorsal rhombomere 1 is initially established by Fgf8 and other signalling molecules originating from the isthmic organizer, a transient embryonic mid/hindbrain junction at neural tube closure (Nakamura et al., 2005; Basson and Wingate, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The cerebellar ventricular zone gives rise to waves of GABAergic neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: The cerebellar ventricular zone gives rise to waves of GABAergic neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells which migrate radially away from the ventricular zone into the developing cerebellar cortex (Seto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells migrate radially away from the ventricular zone into the developing cerebellar cortex.
source: The cerebellar ventricular zone gives rise to waves of GABAergic neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells which migrate radially away from the ventricular zone into the developing cerebellar cortex (Seto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The cerebellar rhombic lip gives rise to cerebellar glutamatergic neurons including cerebellar granule neuron progenitors (GNPs).
source: The cerebellar rhombic lip gives rise to cerebellar glutamatergic neurons including cerebellar granule neuron progenitors (GNPs), which migrate tangentially over the developing anlage to form the external granule layer (EGL).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cerebellar granule neuron progenitors migrate tangentially over the developing anlage to form the external granule layer (EGL).
source: The cerebellar rhombic lip gives rise to cerebellar glutamatergic neurons including cerebellar granule neuron progenitors (GNPs), which migrate tangentially over the developing anlage to form the external granule layer (EGL).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: From the EGL, newly born granule cells migrate inward radially to form the mature internal granule layer.
source: From the EGL, newly born granule cells migrate inward radially to form the mature internal granule layer (Millen and Gleeson, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Transventricular Shh from the choroid plexus regulates cerebellar ventricular zone proliferation from e14.5.
source: Transventricular Shh from the choroid plexus regulates cerebellar ventricular zone proliferation from e14.5 (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Mesenchymal Bmp signals induce the cerebellar rhombic lip around e10.5 in mice.
source: Mesenchymal Bmp signals induce the cerebellar rhombic lip around e10.5 in mice (Alder et al., 1996, 1999; Fernandes et al., 2012; Tong and Kwan, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Meningeal SDF1α has a chemoattractive role in the tangential migration of GNPs away from the rhombic lip to form the EGL from e12.5.
source: Additionally, meningeal SDF1α has a chemoattractive role in both the tangential migration of GNPs away from the rhombic lip to form the EGL from e12.5, as well as a later role in maintaining their proliferative niche adjacent at the pial surface within the EGL (Hartmann et al., 1998; Ma et al., 1998; Zou et al., 1998; Klein et al., 2001; Reiss et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2002; Vilz et al., 2005; Tiveron and Cremer, 2008; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Meningeal SDF1α has a role in maintaining the proliferative niche of GNPs at the pial surface within the EGL.
source: Additionally, meningeal SDF1α has a chemoattractive role in both the tangential migration of GNPs away from the rhombic lip to form the EGL from e12.5, as well as a later role in maintaining their proliferative niche adjacent at the pial surface within the EGL (Hartmann et al., 1998; Ma et al., 1998; Zou et al., 1998; Klein et al., 2001; Reiss et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2002; Vilz et al., 2005; Tiveron and Cremer, 2008; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Foxc1 expression is initiated in the head mesenchyme adjacent to the developing cerebellum at e12.5.
source: Foxc1 expression is initiated in the head mesenchyme adjacent to the developing cerebellum at e12.5.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding in the Results section.

claim: The Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellum is not dramatically affected at e12.5.
source: Although the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellum is not dramatically affected at e12.5, by e18.5 the mutant cerebellum is highly dysmorphic (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding with citation.

claim: By e18.5 the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellum is highly dysmorphic.
source: Although the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellum is not dramatically affected at e12.5, by e18.5 the mutant cerebellum is highly dysmorphic (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding with citation.

claim: Cerebellar anlage size and shape differences were readily apparent at e13.5 in Foxc1−/− mutants.
source: Cresyl violet staining confirmed dramatic rhombic lip and EGL abnormalities (Aldinger et al., 2009) at all stages, however we also noted extensive additional abnormalities of the cerebellar ventricular zone and its derivatives in mutant animals as early at e13.5, when cerebellar anlage size and shape differences were readily apparent (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The posterior fossa mesenchyme in the Foxc1−/− mutant was structurally normal.
source: Unlike the forebrain mesenchyme, the posterior fossa mesenchyme in the Foxc1−/− mutant was structurally normal, as indicated by Laminin, Pdgfr1 and Raldh2 staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At e13.5, Foxc1−/− mutants demonstrated a twofold reduction of ventricular zone proliferation, compared to e13.5 wild-type animals.
source: Dramatically, at e13.5, Foxc1−/− mutants demonstrated a twofold reduction of ventricular zone proliferation, compared to e13.5 wild-type animals.
evidence: This is stated as a quantified finding from BrdU pulse experiments.

claim: At e15.5, ventricular zone proliferation was significantly lower in Foxc1−/− mutants compared to control animals.
source: At e15.5, ventricular zone proliferation was also significantly lower in Foxc1−/− mutants compared to control animals (Figure 1I–M).
evidence: This is stated as a quantified finding from BrdU pulse experiments and supported by Figure 1I-M.

claim: Reduced proliferation in Foxc1−/− mutants was accompanied by a concomitant substantial increase in differentiation as visualized by β-III Tubulin expression.
source: Reduced proliferation in Foxc1−/− mutants was accompanied by a concomitant substantial increase in differentiation as visualized by β-III Tubulin expression, an early marker of differentiating neurons (Brazelton et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding with citation for the marker.

claim: β-III Tubulin is an early marker of differentiating neurons.
source: Reduced proliferation in Foxc1−/− mutants was accompanied by a concomitant substantial increase in differentiation as visualized by β-III Tubulin expression, an early marker of differentiating neurons (Brazelton et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells are generated between e10.5 and e13.5.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje cells are generated between e10.5 and e13.5 (Sudarov et al., 2011) and migrate out of the ventricular zone beginning at e14.5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells migrate out of the ventricular zone beginning at e14.5.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje cells are generated between e10.5 and e13.5 (Sudarov et al., 2011) and migrate out of the ventricular zone beginning at e14.5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: At e15.5 in wild-type animals, Purkinje cells defined by Calbindin-expression are in a domain overlying the ventricular zone.
source: At e15.5 in wild-type animals, we observed Purkinje cells defined by Calbindin-expression in a domain overlying the ventricular zone (Figure 2A,A′, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 2A,A'.

claim: By e19.5 wild-type Purkinje cells had migrated outwards to form a multilayered Purkinje cell plate underneath the external granule layer in the developing cerebellar cortex.
source: By e19.5 these wild-type cells had migrated outwards to form a multilayered Purkinje cell plate underneath the external granule layer in the developing cerebellar cortex (Figure 2C,C′, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 2C,C'.

claim: At e15.5 in Foxc1−/− mutants, fewer Purkinje cells were present.
source: As expected at e15.5 in Foxc1−/− mutants, fewer Purkinje cells were present since proliferation of the ventricular zone was compromised during the peak of Purkinje cell production.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding with inference about the cause.

claim: At e15.5 in Foxc1−/− mutants, most remaining calbindin expressing cells were scattered throughout the anlage.
source: Purkinje cell migration however was also affected. While some cells remained in the ventricular zone at this stage, most remaining calbindin expressing cells were scattered throughout the anlage (Figure 2B,B′, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 2B,B'.

claim: By e19.5 the majority of the mutant Purkinje cells remained within the core of the cerebellar anlage.
source: By e19.5 the majority of the mutant Purkinje cells remained within the core of the cerebellar anlage with just a few present in a residual dysmorphic Purkinje cell plate located in the anterior cerebellum (Figure 2D,D′, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 2D,D'.

claim: Radial glial cells serve as both neuronal progenitors and a scaffold for Purkinje cell neurons as they migrate towards the cerebellar cortex.
source: RG cells serve as both neuronal progenitors (Feng et al., 1994) and a scaffold for Purkinje cell neurons as they migrate towards the cerebellar cortex (Yuasa et al., 1996; Hatten, 1999)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Bergmann glia serve as a scaffold for migrating granule neurons from the EGL.
source: while BG serve as a scaffold for migrating granule neurons from the EGL.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In wild-type animals at e13.5 and e15.5, the nestin-positive soma of RG were located in the ventricular zone with radial fibers extending to the NTZ or pial surface.
source: In wild-type animals at e13.5 and e15.5, the nestin-positive soma of RG were located in the ventricular zone with radial fibers extending to the NTZ or pial surface (Figure 3A, arrows).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: In Foxc1−/− mutants at e13.5, nestin-positive staining was evident; however extended radial fibers were absent.
source: In Foxc1−/− mutants at e13.5, nestin-positive staining was evident; however extended radial fibers were absent (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: By e15.5 nestin-positive fibers were discontinuous with very few extending to the pial surface in Foxc1−/− mutants.
source: By e15.5 nestin-positive fibers were discontinuous with very few extending to the pial surface (Figure 3D,D′, arrows).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3D,D'.

claim: Bergmann glial morphology and arrangement were found to be disrupted in the Foxc1−/− mutant.
source: Additionally, Bergmann glial morphology and arrangement were found to be disrupted in the Foxc1−/− mutant (Figure 3F–H,J–M, Figure 3K,M; arrows).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3F-H,J-M.

claim: In the Foxc1−/− mutant, Bergmann glial cells were found to be present ectopically in the EGL and ML indicating abnormal migration.
source: In the WT, BG were found to overlap with the PL (Figure 3E,G,J,L), while in the Foxc1−/− mutant cells were found to be present ectopically in the EGL and ML indicating abnormal migration (Figure 3K,M).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3K,M.

claim: Increased cell death in the ventricular zone of Foxc1−/− mutants was observed as measured by TUNEL labeling.
source: These changes were accompanied by increased cell death in the ventricular zone of Foxc1−/− mutants as measured by TUNEL labeling (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 3I.

claim: The disruption of radial glial migratory scaffold in Foxc1−/− mutants contributes to aberrant PC migratory phenotypes.
source: Together, our results suggest that the disruption of radial glial migratory scaffold in Foxc1−/− mutants contributes to aberrant PC migratory phenotypes in Foxc1−/− mutant mice, which in turn also contribute to an abnormal BG phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed data.

claim: Aberrant PC migratory phenotypes in turn contribute to an abnormal BG phenotype.
source: Together, our results suggest that the disruption of radial glial migratory scaffold in Foxc1−/− mutants contributes to aberrant PC migratory phenotypes in Foxc1−/− mutant mice, which in turn also contribute to an abnormal BG phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed data.

claim: The embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone does not express Bmp-receptors.
source: The embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone does not express Bmp-receptors although they are expressed in the rhombic lip (Machold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Bmp-receptors are expressed in the rhombic lip.
source: The embryonic cerebellar ventricular zone does not express Bmp-receptors although they are expressed in the rhombic lip (Machold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The SDF1α receptor, Cxcr4 is highly expressed in the embryonic ventricular zone.
source: In contrast, the SDF1α receptor, Cxcr4 is highly expressed in the embryonic ventricular zone (Figure 5 and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Addition of SDF1α significantly increased cell division in primary dissociated cultures of the wild-type e13.5 cerebellar anlage.
source: Addition of SDF1α significantly increased cell division in primary dissociated cultures of the wild-type e13.5 cerebellar anlage.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from in vitro assays.

claim: Blocking SDF1α function using the Cxcr4 receptor antagonist AMD 3100 significantly inhibited BrdU uptake in primary dissociated cultures.
source: Blocking SDF1α function using the Cxcr4 receptor antagonist AMD 3100 (Rosenkilde et al., 2004), significantly inhibited BrdU uptake in these cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from in vitro assays and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: AMD 3100 is a Cxcr4 receptor antagonist.
source: Blocking SDF1α function using the Cxcr4 receptor antagonist AMD 3100 (Rosenkilde et al., 2004), significantly inhibited BrdU uptake in these cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Blockage of the SDF1α-Cxcr4 signalling pathway caused a significant increase in ventricular zone neuronal differentiation.
source: Subsequent sections of these whole mount cerebellar cultures revealed that blockage of the SDF1α-Cxcr4 signalling pathway caused a significant increase in ventricular zone neuronal differentiation and reduced proliferation. (Figure 4A,C–F).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from whole mount culture experiments and supported by Figure 4A,C-F.

claim: Blockage of the SDF1α-Cxcr4 signalling pathway caused reduced proliferation in the ventricular zone.
source: Subsequent sections of these whole mount cerebellar cultures revealed that blockage of the SDF1α-Cxcr4 signalling pathway caused a significant increase in ventricular zone neuronal differentiation and reduced proliferation. (Figure 4A,C–F).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from whole mount culture experiments and supported by Figure 4A,C-F.

claim: SDF1α significantly increased the number of e13.5 dissociated cerebellar cells that migrated through a membrane in a standard transwell migration assay.
source: Indeed, SDF1α significantly increased the number of e13.5 dissociated cerebellar cells that migrated through a membrane in a standard transwell migration assay.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from transwell migration assays.

claim: Addition of AMD 3100 to cells in the upper chamber significantly reduced the number of migrating cells in the transwell assay.
source: Further, addition of AMD 3100 to cells in the upper chamber significantly reduced the number of migrating cells. (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from transwell migration assays and supported by Figure 4G,H.

claim: Td-tomato positive cells were specifically directed towards the source of SDF1α in matrigel migration assays.
source: After 48 hr, Td-tomato positive cells were specifically directed towards the source of SDF1α (Figure 4K,K′,K′′).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from matrigel migration assays and supported by Figure 4K,K',K''.

claim: SDF1α can promote cerebellar ventricular zone progenitor proliferation.
source: Thus, not only can SDF1α promote cerebellar ventricular zone progenitor proliferation, it can also function as a chemoattractant to cerebellar ventricular zone derived cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vitro experimental findings.

claim: SDF1α can function as a chemoattractant to cerebellar ventricular zone derived cells.
source: Thus, not only can SDF1α promote cerebellar ventricular zone progenitor proliferation, it can also function as a chemoattractant to cerebellar ventricular zone derived cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vitro experimental findings.

claim: Cxcl12, the gene encoding SDF1α is a direct target of Foxc1.
source: Cxcl12, the gene encoding SDF1α is a direct target of Foxc1 (Zarbalis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Cxcl12 is expressed in embryonic posterior fossa mesenchyme based on RT-PCR data.
source: It is expressed in embryonic posterior fossa mesenchyme based on RT-PCR data and its expression is reduced in Foxc1−/− mutants (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a previously reported finding with citation.

claim: Cxcl12 expression is reduced in Foxc1−/− mutants.
source: It is expressed in embryonic posterior fossa mesenchyme based on RT-PCR data and its expression is reduced in Foxc1−/− mutants (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a previously reported finding with citation.

claim: SDF1α protein is expressed in mesenchymal cells adjacent to the cerebellar anlage at e13.5.
source: Using a BAC transgenic mouse encoding an SDF1α:mRFP fusion protein (Jung et al., 2009; Mithal et al., 2013), we confirmed that SDF1α protein is expressed in mesenchymal cells adjacent to the cerebellar anlage at e13.5.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding using transgenic reporter mice.

claim: Scattered RFP-positive cells, likely pericytes, were observed within the cerebellar anlage at e13.5.
source: In addition, we observed scattered RFP-positive cells, likely pericytes, within the cerebellar anlage at this stage (Figure 5A, arrow).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: At e13.5, Cxcr4 was expressed around the soma of cells in the ventricular zone, the rhombic lip, the nascent EGL, the NTZ and the pia.
source: At e13.5, Cxcr4 was expressed around the soma of cells in the ventricular zone, the rhombic lip, the nascent EGL, the NTZ and the pia (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Cxcr4 expression was seen in fibers extending out of the ventricular zone towards the pial surface.
source: Strikingly, Cxcr4 expression was also seen in fibers extending out of the ventricular zone towards the pial surface.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding.

claim: Cxcr4-expressing fibers extending from the ventricular zone were nestin-positive and thus are radial glial fibers.
source: These fibers were nestin-positive and thus are radial glial fibers (Figure 5D, arrow).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 5D.

claim: Cxcr4-expressing radial glial fibers persisted at e14.5 and became restricted to the anterior cerebellum by e16.5.
source: As expected of radial glial fibers, they persisted at e14.5 and became restricted to the anterior cerebellum by e16.5 (compare Figure 5F with 3E).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 5F and 3E.

claim: Unlike nestin, Cxcr4 expression was not retained in Bergmann Glial cells of the developing cerebellar cortex.
source: Unlike nestin however, Cxcr4 expression was not retained in Bergmann Glial cells of the developing cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding.

claim: Numbers of BrdU-positive ventricular zone cells were dramatically reduced in the Cxcr4 CKO at e13.5 and e15.5.
source: As seen in Foxc1−/− mutant cerebella, numbers of BrdU-positive ventricular zone cells were also dramatically reduced in the Cxcr4 CKO at e13.5 and e15.5 (Figure 6A–D,I, Graph).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6A-D,I.

claim: There was an extensive increase in numbers of differentiated β-III tubulin positive cells at e13.5 and e15.5 in Cxcr4 CKO.
source: Concurrently, there was an extensive increase in numbers of differentiated β-III tubulin positive cells at e13.5 and e15.5.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding.

claim: Numerous β-III tubulin-positive cells were ectopically interspersed throughout the diminished Cxcr4 CKO mutant ventricular zone at e13.5 and e15.5.
source: Similar to Foxc1 null mutants, numerous β-III tubulin -positive cells were also ectopically interspersed throughout the diminished Cxcr4 CKO mutant ventricular zone at both stages (Figure 6F,H, Boxed area).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6F,H.

claim: Few calbindin-positive Purkinje cells were present at e15.5 in the Cxcr4 CKO.
source: Again, similar to Foxc1−/− mutant few calbindin-positive Purkinje cells were present at e15.5 in the Cxcr4 CKO and those remaining were scattered throughout the anlage and located adjacent to the pia (Figure 6L, arrow), instead of remaining in a domain more closely associated with the ventricular zone as in wild-type cerebella (Figure 6K, arrow).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6K,L.

claim: Long radial glial fibers were not present in the Cxcr4-CKO mutant at e13.5 and e15.5.
source: Although many nestin-positive radial glial cells were present in the Cxcr4-CKO mutant at e13.5 and e15.5, long radial glial fibers were not present at either stage (Figure 6M–P).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6M-P.

claim: Radial glial fibers were still readily detected in the midbrain of Cxcr4-CKO mutants.
source: Notably, radial glial fibers were still readily detected in the midbrain (Figure 6N, arrows).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6N.

claim: Increased cell death was observed in the Cxcr4 CKO ventricular zone compared to control at e13.5 and e15.5.
source: As seen in the Foxc1−/− mutant, increased cell death was also observed in the Cxcr4 CKO ventricular zone compared to control at e13.5 and e15.5 (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6J.

claim: Nests of ectopic proliferating granule cell progenitors were present within the Cxcr4-Nes-Cre mutant cerebellar anlage.
source: In contrast to the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellum however, nests of ectopic proliferating granule cell progenitors were present within the Cxcr4-Nes-Cre mutant cerebellar anlage at this stage, as others have previously reported (Figure 6D, asterisk).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6D.

claim: Bergmann glia were found ectopically located in the EGL in Cxcr4-Nes-Cre mutants similar to the Foxc1−/− mutant.
source: Bergmann glia were found ectopically located in the EGL similar to the Foxc1−/− mutant (Figure 6R, arrows).
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding and supported by Figure 6R.

claim: Loss of Cxcr4 in the nestin-expressing radial glial cells recapitulates multiple aspects of the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellar phenotype.
source: We conclude that loss of Cxcr4 in the nestin-expressing radial glial cells recapitulates multiple aspects of the Foxc1−/− mutant cerebellar phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative phenotypic analysis.

claim: Foxc1-dependent SDF1α secretion by the posterior fossa head mesenchyme and its reception by Cxcr4 in adjacent early cerebellar anlage radial glial cells represent a major downstream effector pathway mediating Foxc1 Dandy-Walker cerebellar pathogenesis.
source: The striking similarities of these mutant cerebellar phenotypes strongly argues that Foxc1-dependent SDF1α secretion by the posterior fossa head mesenchyme and its reception by Cxcr4 in adjacent early cerebellar anlage radial glial cells, represent a major downstream effector pathway mediating Foxc1 Dandy-Walker cerebellar pathogenesis
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined experimental findings.

claim: SDF1α treatment led to a significant increase in proliferation in the VZ of the Foxc1−/− cerebellum.
source: SDF1α treatment did not have any effect on the WT cerebellum (Figure 7A,E,D,H), but led to a significant increase in proliferation in the VZ of the Foxc1−/− cerebellum (Figure 7, Compare 7B with 7A and 7C; 7D Graph).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from rescue experiments and supported by Figure 7.

claim: SDF1α significantly inhibited the early differentiation phenotype in the Foxc1−/− cerebellum.
source: Also, while there were no differences in differentiation levels in the WT cerebellar tissue treated with and without SDF1α (Figure 7E,H), SDF1α significantly inhibited the early differentiation phenotype in the Foxc1−/− cerebellum (Figure 7, Compare 7F with 7G and 7E; 7H Graph).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from rescue experiments and supported by Figure 7.

claim: SDF1α is the major downstream effector of posterior fossa Foxc1.
source: These data reinforce our conclusion that SDF1α is the major downstream effector of posterior fossa Foxc1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the rescue experiments.

claim: The pathogenesis underlying Foxc1-dependent Dandy-Walker malformation is caused by loss of SDF1α-Cxcr4 mediated cerebellar radial glial proliferative and migrational scaffold function.
source: Here we have demonstrated that the pathogenesis underlying Foxc1-dependent Dandy-Walker malformation, a major human neurodevelopmental disorder, is caused by loss of SDF1α-Cxcr4 mediated cerebellar radial glial proliferative and migrational scaffold function.
evidence: This is stated as a major conclusion from the study.

claim: SDF1α function is central to almost every major developmental program of the cerebellum.
source: Thus, SDF1α function is central to almost every major developmental program of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comprehensive analysis of SDF1α functions.

claim: SDF1α is a chemokine, central to the body's inflammatory response.
source: Notably, SDF1α is also a chemokine, central to the body's inflammatory response (Dotan et al., 2010; Werner et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Maternal infection has long been recognized as a risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism which has been associated with cerebellar hypoplasia.
source: Maternal infection has long been recognized as a risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism which has been associated with cerebellar hypoplasia (Fatemi et al., 2008; Buehler, 2011; Burd et al., 2012; Garbett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Neuroinflammation, including misregulated SDF1α signalling during early fetal development may underlie cases of human cerebellar hypoplasia for which genetic mechanisms have been difficult to assign.
source: It is intriguing to speculate that neuroinflammation, including misregulated SDF1α signalling during early fetal development may underlie cases of human cerebellar hypoplasia for which genetic mechanisms have been difficult to assign (Sajan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Radial glial cells in the developing cerebellum are more sensitive to loss of SDF1α signalling compared to other regions of the CNS.
source: Our analysis indicates that radial glial cells in the developing cerebellum are more sensitive to loss of SDF1α signalling compared to other regions of the CNS.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: Loss of SDF1α signalling in the cerebellum causes immediate and catastrophic cell cycle exit of radial glial cells and corresponding increased neuronal differentiation.
source: In the cerebellum, loss of SDF1α signalling causes immediate and catastrophic cell cycle exit of radial glial cells and corresponding increased neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding from the study.

claim: Rapid loss of radial glial fiber morphology is observed with loss of SDF1α signalling in the cerebellum.
source: Rapid loss of radial glial fiber morphology is also observed.
evidence: This is stated as an observed finding from the study.

claim: Loss of SDF1α signalling in the forebrain has not been reported to cause microcephaly in mice.
source: Loss of SDF1α signalling in the forebrain has not been reported to cause microcephaly in mice, and we have shown here that midbrain radial glial cells are relatively unaffected (Figure 6N).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and supported by Figure 6N.

claim: Loss of radial glial Cxcr4 in spinal cord radial glial cells causes disruption of radial glial morphology and reduced mitosis in the ventral ventricular zone by e14.5.
source: A recent study (Mithal et al., 2013) reported that loss of radial glial Cxcr4 in spinal cord radial glial cells causes disruption of radial glial morphology and reduced mitosis in the ventral ventricular zone by e14.5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The disproportionate mouse cerebellar phenotypes with loss of Foxc1 and Cxcr4 model the CNS phenotype of Dandy-Walker malformation patients.
source: The disproportionate mouse cerebellar phenotypes we report here with loss of Foxc1 and Cxcr4 beautifully model the CNS phenotype of Dandy-Walker malformation patients, where the cerebellum is disproportionately diminished in size and altered in morphology relative to other CNS structures.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: Head mesenchyme is a mixture of head mesoderm and head neural crest cells which surrounds the developing brain.
source: Head mesenchyme is a mixture of head mesoderm and head neural crest cells which surrounds the developing brain (Yoshida et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Head mesenchyme differentiates to form all structures between the brain and the epidermis, including the meninges, skull and skin dermis.
source: It differentiates to form all structures between the brain and the epidermis, including the meninges which secretes the pial basement membrane the skull and the skin dermis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Signalling from the head mesenchyme has been implicated in brain regionalization during early neural plate and neural tube stages.
source: Signalling from the head mesenchyme and its derivatives to the developing brain has been implicated in a number of important developmental processes from brain regionalization during early neural plate and neural tube stages (LaMantia et al., 2000; Le Douarin et al., 2012; Andoniadou and Martinez-Barbera, 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Signalling from the head mesenchyme has been implicated in the regulation of tangential migration of Cajal Retzius cells and cortical interneurons.
source: through the regulation of tangential migration of Cajal Retzius cells and cortical interneurons (Kwon et al., 2011; Zarbalis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Physical interactions between the pial surface and the end-feet of radial glial cells are required for radial glial survival, proliferation and maintenance of radial fiber morphology.
source: Physical interactions between the pial surface and the end-feet of radial glial cells are also known to be required for radial glial survival, proliferation as well as maintenance of radial fiber morphology to direct the radial migration of neurons (Radakovits et al., 2009; Siegenthaler and Pleasure, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Bmp, Fgf and Wnts are coordinately required to induce and then caudalize the neural plate and neural tube.
source: For example, Bmp, Fgf and Wnts are coordinately required to induce and then caudalize the neural plate and neural tube (Andoniadou and Martinez-Barbera, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: SDF1α has been shown to regulate tangential migration of cortical neurons.
source: SDF1α, a chemokine has been shown to regulate tangential migration of cortical neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Intact integrins and laminins are required in the pial basement to maintain contact with radial glial endfeet.
source: Intact integrins and laminins are required in the pial basement maintain contact with radial glial endfeet (Radakovits et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Wnt signals derived from the isthmic organizer determine the initial size of the cerebellar anlage from ∼e9.0.
source: Wnt signals derived from both the isthmic organizer (Sato et al., 2004; Sato and Joyner, 2009) and the early dorsal roof plate (Chizhikov et al., 2006) determine the initial size of the anlage from ∼e9.0.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Wnt signals derived from the early dorsal roof plate determine the initial size of the cerebellar anlage from ∼e9.0.
source: Wnt signals derived from both the isthmic organizer (Sato et al., 2004; Sato and Joyner, 2009) and the early dorsal roof plate (Chizhikov et al., 2006) determine the initial size of the anlage from ∼e9.0.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Mesenchymal SDF1α signalling is a major driver of early anlage growth from ∼e12.5.
source: We have now demonstrated that mesenchymal SDF1α signalling is a major driver of early anlage growth from ∼e12.5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Late embryonic anlage ventricular zone proliferation is influenced by Shh derived from the differentiating choroid plexus from e14.5.
source: Late embryonic anlage ventricular zone proliferation is influenced by Shh derived from the differentiating choroid plexus from e14.5 (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: SDF1α secreted by the mesenchyme binds to the receptor on the radial fibers to relay signals that are directly required to maintain these radial fibers as a substrate for migration.
source: We conclude that SDF1α secreted by the mesenchyme binds to the receptor on the radial fibers to relay signals that are directly required to maintain these radial fibers as a substrate for migration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the expression and phenotypic data.

claim: In the spinal cord, SDF1α protein is detectable in radial end feet and transcytosis across the radial glial length is also observed.
source: Indeed in the spinal cord, SDF1α protein is detectable in radial end feet and transcytosis across the radial glial length is also observed (Mithal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Radial glial cells in the cerebellum can differentiate into Bergmann glial cells in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Radial glial cells in the cerebellum can differentiate into Bergmann glial cells (also known as Golgi Epithelial cells) in the cerebellar cortex (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The association of BG with PCs greatly contributes to their structural and functional maintenance.
source: Studies have also shown that the association of BG with PCs greatly contributes to their structural and functional maintenance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Sonic hedgehog secretion by PCs helps maintain BG in the cerebellum.
source: Sonic hedgehog secretion by PCs also helps maintain BG in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Bergmann glial cells are normally born between e13.5 and e14.5 in the mouse cerebellum.
source: Fate mapping studies have shown that Bergmann glial cells are normally born between e13.5 and e14.5 in the mouse cerebellum (Sudarov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: A lack of normal Bergmann glial fibers contributes to the abnormal lamination in neonatal SDF1α and Cxcr4 mutant animals.
source: Regardless, it is certain that a lack of normal Bergmann glial fibers further contributes to the abnormal lamination in neonatal SDF1α and Cxcr4 mutant animals as these fibers are normally required for the inward migration of EGL cells to form the internal granule layer.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observed phenotypes.

claim: Bergmann glial fibers are normally required for the inward migration of EGL cells to form the internal granule layer.
source: Regardless, it is certain that a lack of normal Bergmann glial fibers further contributes to the abnormal lamination in neonatal SDF1α and Cxcr4 mutant animals as these fibers are normally required for the inward migration of EGL cells to form the internal granule layer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.
